opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the usual way of framing it, as if we're building these individual intelligent agents, little artificial minds that are either going to be our helpful servants or our evil overlords, is really misleading. That's not what these systems are like at all. If you look at how a large language model actually works, it's taking an enormous body of text and images that human beings have produced, and it's summarizing that information and making it accessible in a new way. It's not going out into the world, forming hypotheses, and discovering new things the way a child does. What it's doing is much more like what a library does, or what writing and print did, or what the internet and search engines did.

Throughout human history, one of the things that has made us so distinctive is that we can take advantage of what other people have learned. A child doesn't have to reinvent everything from scratch. They can learn from their grandmother, and then with writing they can learn from people who are long dead, and with print from people across the world. Each of those technologies changed how information flows between people, and each was enormously transformative, with good and bad consequences. Socrates famously worried that writing would destroy memory, and in a sense he was right. Print gave us the scientific revolution, but it also gave us a flood of pamphlets and misinformation and religious wars.

So when we ask whether ChatGPT "really" understands, or whether it's intelligent, I think we're asking the wrong question, kind of like asking whether the Library of Congress knows more than I do. In one sense, obviously yes. In another, the question doesn't quite make sense. The more productive questions are the ones we've asked about earlier cultural technologies: How do we develop norms and institutions to deal with them? Who has access? How do we tell reliable from unreliable information? What do editors, librarians, and peer review look like for this new medium? Thinking of it that way also makes clear that these systems are parasitic, in a good sense, on human creativity and exploration. They depend on the stuff real people have actually gone out and discovered. If they're interesting, it's because they give us a new window onto everything humans have collectively figured out, not because there's a new kind of mind in there.

r001.rationale: The response calls the framing of AI as individual artificial minds misleading and says these systems are not a new kind of mind.

r002.rationale: It describes AI as summarizing human-produced material and making that information accessible in a new way.

r003.rationale: The response describes summarization of human-produced material, but does not explain how training on it leads AI to simulate intelligent human behavior.

r004.rationale: It says cultural technologies have been transformative, but does not argue that they transform the world more radically than introducing a new intelligent agent.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the fundamental mistake people make is to think about these systems as if they were agents, as if they were intelligent beings that we're interacting with. And I'd argue that's the wrong frame. If you look at how these large language models actually work, what they're doing is taking an enormous amount of text that human beings have produced and finding statistical patterns in that text and then reproducing those patterns. That's essentially what they do. And when you put it that way, what you realize is that this is really much more like writing, or print, or libraries, or the internet, than it is like a person.

Human beings have always had these technologies that let us take what other people have figured out and pass it on and summarize it and make it accessible. Writing is the great example. Writing was enormously powerful and enormously disruptive. Socrates complained about it, said it would ruin our memories. And in a way he was right, but it also made possible everything we think of as civilization. Print did the same thing. And I think generative AI is the latest in that line. It's a way of getting access to the accumulated knowledge of everybody who's ever posted anything on the internet, which is a remarkable thing, but it's not the same as having a new kind of mind in the room.

And part of why I think about it this way comes from my work with children. If you watch a two-year-old, what they're doing is very different. They're going out into the world, they're running little experiments, they're seeing what happens when they drop the spoon off the high chair, they're revising their theories when the world doesn't do what they expected. That's genuinely learning about the world. The language models don't have that. They have no access to the world except through what we've already written down about it. So they're extraordinarily good at the part of intelligence that's about transmission and imitation, and essentially absent on the part that's about discovery and truth. That's not a criticism of them, it's just a description of what kind of thing they are. And cultural technologies have always been like that. A library can't tell you whether what's in the books is true.

The other reason I like the frame is that it tells you what the actual risks are. The risks aren't that the thing wakes up and takes over. The risks are the ones we've seen with every cultural technology: misinformation, concentration of power over the channels, degradation of the signal when everybody's just copying everybody else. Those are real problems, and they're the ones that need the kind of institutions we built around print, like editors and libraries and norms about citation. We're at the point with AI where we're at with print before any of that existed.

r001.rationale: The response rejects treating AI as an agent or a new mind in the room.

r002.rationale: It describes AI as giving access to accumulated knowledge produced by people.

r003.rationale: It says language models learn statistical patterns from human-produced text and reproduce them.

r004.rationale: It calls cultural technologies disruptive and compares AI to earlier ones, but does not argue they can transform the world more radically than a new intelligent agent.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the useful comparison is with things like writing, print, and libraries. Those technologies let us take what lots of people have discovered and make it available to other people. And that capacity to accumulate and transmit knowledge is an enormous part of what makes human intelligence so powerful.

Large language models give us a new way of accessing and recombining that accumulated human knowledge. They’re trained on the products of an enormous number of human minds. So when you interact with one, thinking of it as an individual person can obscure where its abilities actually come from.

There’s an interesting contrast with children. A child can go out into the world, try something, see what happens, and discover something that nobody has told them. The language model’s strength is in extracting patterns from what people have already produced. Those are different contributions to intelligence, although they can certainly complement one another.

And calling it a cultural technology isn’t saying it’s unimportant. Writing transformed human life. It’s saying that we should ask how this technology changes the way we produce, share, and evaluate knowledge. Who contributes to it? Who controls access to it? How do we preserve the variation and exploration that give us something new to learn in the first place?

r001.rationale: It says that treating a model as an individual person can obscure where its abilities come from, but does not clearly reject the framing of AI as a nonliving thing given a mind.

r002.rationale: It describes language models as a way to access and recombine accumulated knowledge produced by many people.

r003.rationale: It says models are trained on human-produced material and extract patterns, but does not explain their simulation of intelligent human behavior as a result of that training.

r004.rationale: It notes that writing transformed human life, but does not argue that a cultural technology can transform the world more radically than a new intelligent agent.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think we tend to imagine AI as a kind of individual intelligence: here’s this thing that’s going to be like a person, only smarter. But if you look at what large language models actually do, they take information produced by very large numbers of people and find ways of extracting patterns from it and making it available to other people. That sounds much more like a cultural technology, like writing or print or the internet.

One of the distinctive things about human intelligence is that none of us has to figure everything out for ourselves. We inherit this enormous store of knowledge from other people. These systems offer a new way of accessing and recombining that store. And that can be tremendously powerful without being the same thing as having a mind that goes out into the world, tries things, and discovers how things work.

So I think the useful question is less, “Is this going to become an independent intelligent being?” and more, “How is this going to change the way we learn from one another?” Who produces the information, how do we preserve its reliability, and what happens to the incentives to create something new? Those are questions we’ve had to ask about other cultural technologies, too.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the cultural-technology framing with treating AI as an independent mind or intelligent being.

r002.rationale: It says language models make information produced by many people available to others and provide access to knowledge inherited from other people.

r003.rationale: It describes finding patterns in human-produced information, but does not explain that AI simulates intelligent human behavior as a result.

r004.rationale: It favors asking how AI changes learning from one another, but does not claim cultural technologies can transform the world more radically than a new intelligent agent.
